fetched_contents.text: The Effect of Hydration on Urine Color Objectively Evaluated in CIE L*a*b* Color Space Abstract Urine color has been shown to be a viable marker of hydration status in healthy adults. Traditionally, urine color has been measured using a subjective color scale. In recent years, tristimulus colorimetry developed by the International Commission on Illumination (CIE L*a*b*) has been widely adopted as the reference method for color analysis. In the L*a*b* color space, L* indicates lightness ranging from 100 (white) to 0 (black), while a* and b* indicate chromaticity. a* and b* are color directions: –a* is the green axis, +a* is the red axis, –b* is the blue axis, and +b* is the yellow axis. The L*a*b* color space model is only accurately represented in three-dimensional space. Considering the above, the purpose of the current study was to evaluate urine color during different hydration states, with the results expressed in CIE L*a*b* color space. The study included 28 healthy participants (22 males and 6 females) ranging between the age of 20 and 67 years (28.6 ± 11.3 years). One hundred and fifty-one urine samples were collected from the subjects in various stages of hydration, including morning samples after 7–15 h of water deprivation. Osmolality and CIE L*a*b* parameters were measured in each sample. As the urine osmolality increased, a significant linear increase in b* values was observed as the samples became more pronouncedly yellow (τb = 0.708). An increase in dehydration resulted in darker and significantly more yellow urine, as L* values decreased in lightness and b* values increased along the blue–yellow axis. However, as dehydration increased, a notable polynomial trend in color along the green–red axis was observed as a* values initially decreased, indicating a green hue in slightly dehydrated urine, and then increased as urine became more concentrated and thus more dehydrated. It was determined that 74% of the variance seen in urine osmolality was due to CIE L*a*b* variables. This newfound knowledge about urine color change along with the presented regression model for predicting urine osmolality provides a more detailed and objective perspective on the effect of hydration on urine color, which to our knowledge has not been previously researched. Keywords: urine color, urine osmolality, dehydration, color space, CIE L*a*b* Introduction Urine color has been shown to be a viable marker of hydration status in healthy adults (1, 2). This is evidenced by the significant correlations (r > 0.70) of urine color with several established physiological measures of whole-body hydration, including urine osmolality and urine-specific gravity (1, 3–5). Urine color is dictated by the concentration of urochrome, a yellow-pigmented waste by-product of hemoglobin catabolism (1, 6, 7). During whole-body dehydration, urochrome concentration increases as antidiuresis is stimulated via increased arginine vasopressin production, thus increasing water reabsorption from the collecting duct of the nephron. This physiological response to dehydration results in darker and more concentrated urine (3, 4). Traditionally, the assessment of hydration through urine color analysis has been performed with a subjective eight-point color scale (1, 3–5). This technique involves visual color matching of a collected urine sample to a stepwise color chart, resulting in an assigned value ranging from 1 (pale yellow) to 8 (dark greenish brown) (3, 4). Color assessments based on visual comparisons to a set of stepwise color samples, also referred to as color-order systems, are known to have several methodological limitations. These include the following: (1) variability of color vision in different individuals, (2) change of color vision with age, (3) potential color blindness in individuals, (4) difficulty in standardization of illumination conditions, and (5) difficulty in standardization of reference color charts (8–10). Furthermore, evidence of the eight-point color scale's success in determining hydration status in older populations is inconclusive (11, 12). Although the eight-point color scale has proven to be a practical tool for convenient assessment of hydration status in healthy adults (1, 3–5), it lacks the capability to be used as a universally accurate tool for objective quantification of urine color. CIE L*a*b* is a system of objective tristimulus colorimetry developed by the International Commission on Illumination (i.e., Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage, CIE) in which three different characteristics constitute a color's position within a three-dimensional color space. CIE L*a*b* analysis describes all colors visible to the human eye and was created to serve as a device-independent reference model. This system has been used to perform objective analysis of color and color movement in several different scientific fields, ranging from food science to medicine. Previous research has used CIE L*a*b* to identify photosynthetic pigmentation in olive oils, to create ranges of human gingival color, and to visualize body movement captured by remote photoplethysmography (13–15). Furthermore, the CIE L*a*b* color space has been widely adopted as a standard for color assessment and quantification since its conception in 1976 (10, 14, 16). In the L*a*b* color space, L* indicates lightness ranging from 100 (white) to 0 (black), while a* and b* indicate chromaticity or the quality of a color independent of its luminance. a* and b* are color directions: –a* is the green axis, +a* is the red axis, –b* is the blue axis, and +b* is the yellow axis. As the L*a*b* color space is a three-dimensional model, it can only be accurately represented in a three-dimensional space (Figure 1). fetched_contents.text: Urine-Specific Gravity: Purpose, Range & High Symptoms How does specific gravity of urine work? You provide a urine sample — that is, you pee in a cup — and a healthcare provider will insert a dipstick into your sample. A dipstick is a thin strip of plastic or paper with patches of chemicals. The chemicals change color according to the specific gravity of your pee. In some cases, a provider may insert a few drops of your urine sample into a refractometer. A refractometer is a medical device that shows how much light passes through pee. It’s more accurate than a dipstick. If you have a lot of water in your pee, more light passes through your urine sample. If you have more waste products in your pee, less light will pass. What to expect before a specific gravity of urine test? A healthcare provider will review your medical history and ask you questions. Be sure to tell them about all prescription and over-the-counter medications you’re taking, including herbal supplements. In some cases, you may need to stop taking certain medications shortly before the test because they may affect your results. Don’t stop taking any medications unless a provider specifically says you should. You should also let a provider know if you’ve had any recent imaging tests or procedures that require anesthesia. Anesthesia and imaging tests that use contrast dyes, such as an MRI or CT scan, can affect your urine gravity. A provider will call you ahead of your test with precise directions. You may need to limit how much fluid you drink for at least 12 hours before a specific gravity of urine test. What to expect during specific gravity of urine? You’ll usually provide a urine sample at a healthcare provider’s office or lab. It’s important to wash your hands with soap and water before you pee in the cup. Let your provider know if you have difficulty peeing away from home (shy bladder syndrome). They may give you a cup you can take home or suggest another option that’s more comfortable for you. You should also let them know if you’re getting your period (menstruating). Menstrual blood can affect your specific gravity of urine. Your provider will tell you what to do with your sample once you finish. You may hand it to another provider or leave it in a collection cupboard. What to expect after specific gravity of urine? After you provide your urine sample, a healthcare provider will immediately run a dipstick test or send it to a lab to examine with a refractometer.

Dark urine in the context of dehydration is best understood as a sign of concentrated urine resulting from reduced fluid availability. The evidence directly links dehydration to darker, more yellow urine. In a study evaluating urine color objectively using CIE L*a*b* color space, increased dehydration was associated with darker and significantly more yellow urine, with L* values decreasing in lightness and b* values increasing along the blue–yellow axis [N1-F1]. The same study explains that this happens because urochrome concentration rises during whole-body dehydration, driven by antidiuresis and increased arginine vasopressin production, which increases water reabsorption in the nephron [N1-F1]. Another source states that urine color has been shown to be a viable marker of hydration status in healthy adults, with darker urine indicating more concentrated urine [N1-R2]. A urine-specific gravity source also notes that dehydration, overhydration, or certain conditions may cause urine specific gravity to be outside the normal range, underscoring that urine concentration is a key indicator of hydration state [N3-R2].

The clinical significance of dark urine compared to other dehydration signs is important because it is a visible and easily observed sign, but it is not always sufficient on its own to confirm dehydration. Mayo Clinic notes that dark-colored urine is one of the key symptoms of dehydration, along with extreme thirst, urinating less, tiredness, dizziness, and confusion [N5-R5]. The same source also cautions that dark urine can be caused by other conditions, including liver and kidney disorders and some urinary tract infections, and that dark brown urine may indicate more serious issues [N1-R2]. Similarly, the differential-diagnosis evidence points to bilirubin accumulation in diseases that affect urine color, and to kidney disease or kidney failure as a cause of dark brown urine [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Finally, the urine colour chart evidence says medium-dark yellow urine is an indication of dehydration and that darker, strong-smelling urine is a sign of dehydration, while also noting that urine color can be influenced by foods, medications, and supplements [N3-R5][N4-F3].

The evidence identifies liver and kidney disorders, urinary tract infections, bilirubin-related disease, and even medication side effects as alternative explanations for dark urine [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R5]. A patient with dark urine may have dehydration, but they may also have a more serious underlying condition that requires further investigation [N1-R2][N5-R2]. ## Dark urine: what it means and how to understand it

A study using objective colorimetry explains that during whole-body dehydration, urochrome concentration increases, which makes urine darker and more concentrated [N1-F1].

### Why dark urine matters in dehydration

Dark urine is important because it is a visible sign that your body may be losing fluids faster than it is replacing them. The evidence says that when dehydration occurs, urine becomes more concentrated and turns darker in color [N1-R2][N2-R3]. The physician’s initial explanation is accurate: dark-colored urine is one of the key signs of dehydration, along with thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, and decreased urination [N5-R5].

But dark urine is not always enough by itself. The evidence also shows that other conditions can make urine dark or brown, which is why it matters to distinguish dehydration from other causes. Mayo Clinic notes that dark-colored urine can be a sign of dehydration, but it also can be caused by liver and kidney disorders and some urinary tract infections [N1-R2]. The differential-diagnosis evidence adds that bilirubin accumulation can skew urine toward a brown-orange hue, and that kidney disease or kidney failure can cause urine to turn dark brown [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Healthdirect similarly notes that dark urine can be caused by foods, medications, and vitamin supplements even when a person is hydrated [N4-F3]. So dark urine is a clue, but not a diagnosis on its own.

### How to interpret dark urine in a real patient case

In practice, dark urine should be interpreted alongside other symptoms and the patient’s history. The evidence shows that dehydration is often associated with thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache, and reduced urination [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Cleveland Clinic notes that feeling thirsty already indicates mild dehydration and can cause signs like headache, fatigue, dizziness, and more [N2-R1]. Harvard Health adds that dehydrated urine is more concentrated and becomes darker in color, and that dizziness can occur because dehydration reduces blood volume [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic similarly lists dark-colored urine, extreme thirst, urinating less, tiredness, dizziness, and confusion as symptoms of dehydration [N5-R5].

That means dark urine is more meaningful when it appears with other signs of dehydration. However, dark urine alone is not enough to suspect dehydration. The evidence clearly states that dark urine can also be caused by other conditions, including liver and kidney disorders, urinary tract infections, and even medication side effects [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4]. Healthdirect also emphasizes that dark urine can be influenced by foods, medications, and supplements [N4-F3]. So in a real patient case, you should ask: does the person have a recent history of vomiting, diarrhea, excessive sweating, or exposure to heat? Do they have a history of liver or kidney disease? Are they taking anything that might change urine color? Those details matter a lot.

Dark urine alone is not always enough to suspect dehydration. It is a useful sign, but it should be considered in context. If a patient has recently been exercising, sweating, vomiting, or exposed to heat, and they also have dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache, or reduced urination, the likelihood of dehydration increases [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. That means dark urine should not be ignored, especially if it persists after drinking water.

If dark urine persists after drinking water, it is reasonable to seek medical help [N4-R4].

So the best way to understand dark urine is:  
- **It can be a sign of dehydration**, especially when urine is dark and concentrated [N1-F1][N1-R2].  
- **It can also be caused by other conditions**, so it should not be interpreted in isolation [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].  
- **The best response is to drink more water if hydration is suspected**, but to also consider the full picture of symptoms and history [N3-R5][N4-F3][N4-R3].

## Dark urine: what it means and how to understand it

Dark urine is one of the body’s most visible signals that you may be dehydrated. In short, it happens when your urine becomes more concentrated because your body has less fluid to dilute it. The evidence supports this clearly: increased dehydration is associated with darker and more yellow urine, and urine color has been shown to be a viable marker of hydration status in healthy adults [N1-F1][N1-R2]. A study using objective colorimetry explains that during whole-body dehydration, urochrome concentration increases, which makes urine darker and more concentrated [N1-F1].

### Why dark urine matters in dehydration

Dark urine is important because it is a visible sign that your body may be losing fluids faster than it is replacing them. The evidence says that when dehydration occurs, urine becomes more concentrated and turns darker in color [N1-R2][N2-R3]. The physician’s initial explanation is accurate: dark-colored urine is one of the key signs of dehydration, along with thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, and decreased urination [N5-R5].

But dark urine is not always enough by itself. The evidence also shows that other conditions can make urine dark or brown, which is why it matters to distinguish dehydration from other causes. Mayo Clinic notes that dark-colored urine can be a sign of dehydration, but it also can be caused by liver and kidney disorders and some urinary tract infections [N1-R2]. The differential-diagnosis evidence adds that bilirubin accumulation can skew urine toward a brown-orange hue, and that kidney disease or kidney failure can cause urine to turn dark brown [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Healthdirect similarly notes that dark urine can be caused by foods, medications, and vitamin supplements even when a person is hydrated [N4-F3]. So dark urine is a clue, but not a diagnosis on its own.

### How to interpret dark urine in a real patient case

In practice, dark urine should be interpreted alongside other symptoms and the patient’s history. The evidence shows that dehydration is often associated with thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache, and reduced urination [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Cleveland Clinic notes that feeling thirsty already indicates mild dehydration and can cause signs like headache, fatigue, dizziness, and more [N2-R1]. Harvard Health adds that dehydrated urine is more concentrated and becomes darker in color, and that dizziness can occur because dehydration reduces blood volume [N2-R3]. Mayo Clinic similarly lists dark-colored urine, extreme thirst, urinating less, tiredness, dizziness, and confusion as symptoms of dehydration [N5-R5].

That means dark urine is more meaningful when it appears with other signs of dehydration. However, dark urine alone is not enough to suspect dehydration. The evidence clearly states that dark urine can also be caused by other conditions, including liver and kidney disorders, urinary tract infections, and even medication side effects [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4]. Healthdirect also emphasizes that dark urine can be influenced by foods, medications, and supplements [N4-F3]. So in a real patient case, you should ask: does the person have a recent history of vomiting, diarrhea, excessive sweating, or exposure to heat? Do they have a history of liver or kidney disease? Are they taking anything that might change urine color? Those details matter a lot.

Dark urine alone is not always enough to suspect dehydration. It is a useful sign, but it should be considered in context. If a patient has recently been exercising, sweating, vomiting, or exposed to heat, and they also have dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache, or reduced urination, the likelihood of dehydration increases [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The evidence also shows that persistent dark urine can be a sign of more serious underlying issues, such as cirrhosis or kidney failure [N5-R4]. That means dark urine should not be ignored, especially if it persists after drinking water.

Distinguishing dehydration from other causes of dark urine depends on history, associated symptoms, and context. The evidence points to several alternative explanations: liver disease, kidney disease, kidney failure, urinary tract infections, and bilirubin-related disease [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. The urine-specific gravity evidence also highlights that dehydration can cause urine specific gravity to be outside the normal range, which is a measure of urine concentration [N3-R2][N3-R3]. 1. **Check other signs of dehydration** such as thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache, and decreased urination [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5].
2. **Consider the history** of illness, vomiting, diarrhea, heat exposure, or recent medications [N1-R1][N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].
3. **Think about other causes** such as liver disease, kidney disease, kidney failure, urinary tract infections, or medication side effects [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].
4. **Ask whether dark urine persists after drinking water** [N4-F3][N4-R4].

The evidence supports this clearly: increased dehydration is associated with darker and more yellow urine, and urine color has been shown to be a viable marker of hydration status in healthy adults [N1-F1][N1-R2]. A study using objective colorimetry explains that during whole-body dehydration, urochrome concentration increases, which makes urine darker and more concentrated [N1-F1].

Dark urine is important because it is a visible sign that your body may be losing fluids faster than it is replacing them. The evidence says that when dehydration occurs, urine becomes more concentrated and turns darker in color [N1-R2][N2-R3]. The physician’s initial explanation is accurate: dark-colored urine is one of the key signs of dehydration, along with thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, and decreased urination [N5-R5].

But dark urine is not always enough by itself. The evidence also shows that other conditions can make urine dark or brown, which is why it matters to distinguish dehydration from other causes. Mayo Clinic notes that dark-colored urine can be a sign of dehydration, but it also can be caused by liver and kidney disorders and some urinary tract infections [N1-R2]. The differential-diagnosis evidence adds that bilirubin accumulation can skew urine toward a brown-orange hue, and that kidney disease or kidney failure can cause urine to turn dark brown [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Healthdirect similarly notes that dark urine can be caused by foods, medications, and vitamin supplements even when a person is hydrated [N4-F3]. So dark urine is a clue, but not a diagnosis on its own.

### How to interpret dark urine in a real patient case

In practice, dark urine should be interpreted alongside other symptoms and the patient’s history. The evidence shows that dehydration is often associated with thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache, and reduced urination [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. The evidence supports seeking medical help if dark urine does not go away after drinking water. Healthline advises speaking with a doctor if dark urine persists because the doctor can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment plan [N4-R4]. Mayo Clinic similarly notes that dark-colored urine is a symptom of dehydration but can also be caused by other conditions, which is why persistent dark urine should not be ignored [N1-R2][N5-R5]. The urine-specific gravity evidence also implies that if dark urine persists despite increased fluid intake, further testing may be needed to assess hydration status and rule out other causes [N3-R2][N3-R3].

### Bottom line

Dark urine is a sign that your urine is more concentrated, which often means you are dehydrated [N1-F1][N1-R2]. But it is not always enough on its own to confirm dehydration. Other conditions—including liver disease, kidney disease, kidney failure, urinary tract infections, and medication side effects—can also cause dark or brown urine [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. In a real patient case, dark urine should be interpreted alongside other symptoms such as thirst, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache, and decreased urination [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R5]. If dark urine persists after drinking water, it is reasonable to seek medical help [N4-R4].

So the best way to understand dark urine is:  
- **It can be a sign of dehydration**, especially when urine is dark and concentrated [N1-F1][N1-R2].  
- **It can also be caused by other conditions**, so it should not be interpreted in isolation [N1-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].  
- **The best response is to drink more water if hydration is suspected**, but to also consider the full picture of symptoms and history [N3-R5][N4-F3][N4-R3].
